article.body:
Good morning from Bracketology HQ, and congratulations to Virginia, your national champion. The Cavaliers beat Seton Hall 121-105 in the title game to finish 39-1, and they did it the hard way, with a bracket full of landmines. Let me take you through the whole thing.

THE CHAMPION
Virginia went 6-0 in the tournament and scored 111 points a game doing it. Five of its six wins came by double digits: 97-67 over North Dakota, 117-80 over UAB, 112-72 over Florida State, 113-103 over Texas in the Final Four, and 121-105 over Seton Hall in the final. The one scare was the Elite Eight, where Purdue, a perfect 20-0 team in the Big Ten, took the Cavaliers to the final possession and lost 106-105. That's the whole story of Virginia's year: a team that won its last 38 games in a row, and had to survive exactly one coin flip to get there. The best team in the sim won the title, and for a committee that put it at the top of the board all year, I'll take it.

THE FINAL FOUR
Three No. 1 seeds and a 2 made it to the last weekend. Virginia beat Texas, and Seton Hall edged Alabama 109-107 in the game of the tournament, a game that could have gone either way. The Pirates were the story of the second half of the bracket. They beat Northeastern 107-77, Saint Peter's 115-106 and New Mexico State 106-73, then won two straight by a total of three points, 80-79 over Virginia Tech and that 109-107 win over the Tide. They averaged nearly 104 points a game and still came up 16 short in the final. Alabama (35-4) and Texas (34-5) both ran into teams that simply scored more than they did.

THE ELITE EIGHT
It was a one-possession round. Virginia 106, Purdue 105. Seton Hall 80, Virginia Tech 79. Texas beat Michigan St. 84-80, and Alabama beat San Diego State 94-87. Two of the tournament's four one-point finishes came in this round.

THE SWEET 16 AND ROUND OF 32
The bracket cracked open on Day 50 and Day 51. Virginia Tech, an 8 seed, beat 1 seed Utah St. 99-93, the team that had lost only twice all year, and then beat North Carolina 78-77. New Mexico State, an 11 seed, beat Texas Tech 91-89. Eastern Washington, a 13, beat West Virginia. Michigan St. beat UC Irvine 76-66 and then 2 seed Florida 83-80. San Diego State beat Baylor in the Sweet 16, and Duke handled Kansas 79-63 before Alabama ended its run, 109-72.

THE UPSET TALLY
Twenty of the 63 games after the First Four went to the lower seed. Twelve of them came in the first round, four in the round of 32, three in the Sweet 16 and one in the Final Four, when 2 seed Seton Hall beat 1 seed Alabama. The Elite Eight and the title game went chalk. The tournament averaged a 16.7-point margin, and nine games were decided by three points or fewer. The only two games decided by 40 or more were Purdue's 115-68 win over Vermont and Virginia's 112-72 win over Florida State.

THE CINDERELLAS
Michigan St. is the one I'll remember. The Spartans were 18-14 with an 8-12 Big Ten record, one of the last two at-large teams in the field, and they went to Dayton and won four games to reach the Elite Eight. They beat Wyoming, Indiana, UC Irvine and Florida before a four-point loss to Texas ended the run. The committee took a lot of heat for that selection, and the Spartans answered it. Virginia Tech was the other one. A 24-10 team that went to the ACC final, it beat a 1 seed and a 4 seed and then lost to eventual finalist Seton Hall by a single point. New Mexico State, which also came out of Dayton, won three games, and Eastern Washington, a 13 seed, beat West Virginia to reach the Sweet 16. Credit those four.

THE BUSTS
Utah St. (31-2) is the biggest. A No. 1 seed, 30 points a game in margin, and gone in the second round. Iowa St. and UNLV, both 3 seeds, lost to 14 seeds in the first round, Penn over UNLV 86-81 and UC Irvine over the Cyclones 81-66. Every 7 seed went home in round one, and the 12 seeds went 0-4. Tennessee St., the 32-1 team that I circled as my upset special, lost to Missouri by 17.

THE CONFERENCES
The ACC won 16 games, the most of any league, powered by Virginia's six and Virginia Tech's three. The SEC won 11 and the Big Ten 10, with Michigan St. and Purdue doing most of the work. The Big East got five wins from Seton Hall alone, and the Mountain West won five games, three of them San Diego State's.

HOW MY BRACKET HELD UP
I got the champion right, and I had two of the four Final Four teams, Virginia and Alabama. I missed on Texas and Seton Hall, because I had Florida and Utah St. there instead, and both went out early. By round I was 20 of 32, 10 of 16, 6 of 8 and 2 of 4, so 38 of 60 through the Elite Eight, with the right winner at the end. That's a bracket that was good where the top seeds mattered and wrong wherever a 7-10 or a 13 seed got hot.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This was a tournament of one-possession games, a champion who earned it, and a last-team-in that nearly made the Final Four. If you want to know what to take from it, here it is: the best team won, and nobody should ever tell you that a bubble team can't make a run. See you next season.
